shipped.warum: In October 1884 a company in Edinburgh contracted for 47,000 acres on Sarasota Bay, “below the frost line”. In the same year a vigilance committee of settlers killed Harrison T. Riley and the postmaster Charles E. Abbe; Florida's courts convicted its leaders. In December 1885 Scottish colonists landed; in January snow fell, and by February the colony had broken up.
shipped.quelle: The Economist 1884; Florida Reports 1886 and 1888; The Pensacolian and The Atlanta Constitution 1885; Chicago Daily Tribune 1886; Florida gazetteer 1886–87; Time (London) 1887; Grismer (1946).

planned.warum: After the colony: a hotel for winter guests, a golf course laid out by the company's Scottish manager, the freeze of 1895, a directory of 1897 that lists six Black residents beside the white ones, and the mass meeting of October 1902 that made the village a town.
planned.quelle: Florida gazetteers 1886–87 and 1895; Manatee River Journal 1888–1902; Grismer (1946).

planned.warum: The railroad reached Sarasota in 1903. Winter residents with great fortunes followed: Bertha Palmer of Chicago from 1910, John Ringling of the circus from 1911. From about 1914 Black families built homes in Newtown, outside the town.
planned.quelle: Manatee River Journal 1903–1921; Bradentown City Directory 1916 (with Sarasota); census 1910 and 1920; Grismer (1946).

planned.warum: In 1921 Sarasota became the seat of its own county. In the same year a hurricane struck the waterfront and a former convict guard was held for the murder of a Black prisoner. In the boom of 1925–26 lots, hotels and islands were sold, the causeway to the keys opened, the Klan paraded, and a hotel for Black tourists was planned.
planned.quelle: Manatee River Journal 1921; Monthly Weather Review, October 1921; promotional booklets of about 1922 and 1924; Sarasota Herald, October 1925 to August 1926.

planned.warum: The boom ended in 1926. In the years that followed the celery fields of Palmer Farms, worked mostly by Black labourers, the trailer camps of winter visitors, the Civilian Conservation Corps at Myakka, and the Works Progress Administration's auditorium and beach casino carried the town; the Ringling museum and art school opened.
planned.quelle: Census 1930; Ship-canal hearings 1937; Myakka Rattler (CCC camp paper) 1934–35; Florida state park reports; National Youth Administration directory 1936; Grismer (1946).

planned.warum: From 1942 an Army air base stood east of the town, with more than 3,000 men at its peak; it closed on 2 January 1946. In the same year Karl H. Grismer published The Story of Sarasota: the history a town tells about itself, and what it leaves out.
planned.quelle: Florida newspapers 1942–45; USGS Sarasota quadrangle 1944; Grismer (1946).

missing.warum: The town's own weekly is not digitized. A survey of 1995 lists two issues at the University of South Florida and a run from 1910 to 1924 with the city's historical resources department. Until it can be read, the apparatus relies on the newspaper of Bradentown and on papers elsewhere.

missing.kurz: The bust in its own record
missing.warum: The digitized Sarasota Herald ends in August 1926. For the collapse of the boom, the hurricane of September 1926, the Depression and the town's debts, no public-domain local source has been found yet; Grismer speaks only of a mayor who “succeeded in refunding the city's debt”.

missing.kurz: The colony in the Scottish press
missing.warum: The company's pamphlet of 1885 and the Scottish newspapers that reported the colonists' complaints (the North British Mail, January 1886) are not reachable here; the British Newspaper Archive is paid. They are known through American reprints.
The colonist's memoirs were lent to Grismer as a family manuscript. Only the passages Grismer printed in 1946 are used; a part printed in 1999 is protected.

missing.kurz: The prisoner killed at Salt Springs, 1921
missing.warum: A newspaper of June 1921 reports that a former convict guard, J. R. Bunkley, was held for the murder of a Black prisoner at Salt Springs and bound over to the grand jury of Sarasota County. The prisoner is not named and the outcome has not been found.
No public-domain source before 1946 has been found on who was allowed on Sarasota's beaches. Later reports (1955–56) are named only as pointers.

The Sarasota Herald of 1925–26 records William Selby and his wife as winter residents from Marietta, Ohio. Their arrival, their house on the bay and the gardens that bear Marie Selby's name lie outside what the sources read so far can carry; a chapter of its own is left open.
The Ringling museum (opened 1931) and the art school are documented here only in passing. The painters, classes and exhibitions of the 1930s and 1940s are left open for a chapter of their own.
The Federal Writers' Project guide has a long entry on Sarasota, but its copyright was renewed in 1967. It is not quoted here.

The colonist John Lawrie of Paisley wrote the letter of complaint that the New-York Tribune printed in January 1886 and the Scottish papers copied. The New York paper is on Chronicling America, which is not reachable here; a summary in the Los Angeles Times of 17 January 1886 is too worn in the scan to be read reliably.

missing.kurz: Harrison T. Riley and Charles E. Abbe
missing.warum: Both murdered men appear in the sources only through their killers, the courts and the press. What Riley was accused of comes from the committee itself; why Abbe was hated is disputed in the press of 1885. A genealogy of the Abbe family (1916) and the post office records have not yet been read against the page image.
missing.quelle: Abbe-Abbey Genealogy (1916); records of the Post Office Department.

missing.warum: The Supreme Court's opinions affirm the judgments but do not state the sentences, and what became of the convicted men — pardons, commutations, escapes — is not documented in the sources read so far. The records of the Florida Board of Pardons and the state prison would be needed.

The Calusa, the Cuban and Spanish fishing ranchos on the bay, the Seminole wars and the Whitakers' settlement of the 1840s are told here only in passing. The federal documents on the fishing ranchos of the 1830s and the naval records of the Civil War on the bay have been found but not yet read against the page image.
missing.quelle: Congressional documents of the 1830s; Official Records of the Union and Confederate Navies, vol. 17 (1903).
